notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from the sources I've gathered. I have rich material from Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic), Precept Austin (evangelical), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist), Ellicott's Commentary, Barnes' Notes, the BibleHub summary, and partial Pulpit Commentary/Lange.

---

# Ecclesiastes 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is a collection of proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly, with special attention to how folly operates in everyday life, in speech, in work, and especially in government. Solomon "pivots away from his 'under the sun' meaninglessness toward a call for wisdom and responsibility" (Enduring Word). Barnes notes the chapter "resembles a portion of the Book of Proverbs" and "the thought which underlies the whole chapter is the advantage of that wisdom which includes piety and patience."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/ecclesiastes/10.htm

---

## v. 1 — A Little Folly Spoils Wisdom

**Traditional reading:** As dead flies ruin expensive perfume, so a single foolish act can destroy a reputation built over a lifetime of wisdom and honor. The point is disproportion: the fly is tiny compared to the ointment, yet its stench overwhelms the fragrance. "It only takes one little mistake to ruin a life of great wisdom" (Precept Austin). The verse follows directly from 9:18, "one sinner destroys much good."

Ellicott notes the Hebrew reads literally "flies of death," which could mean "death-giving or poisonous flies," but the traditional rendering "dead flies" yields satisfactory sense. Gill observes that "a good name is like precious ointment, valuable and fragrant; sin, which is folly, is like a dead fly." JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) adds: "The more delicate the perfume, the more easily spoiled is the ointment… so the higher a man's religious character is, the more hurt is caused by a sinful folly in him."

Kidner (quoted in Enduring Word): "There are endless instances of prizes forfeited and good beginning marred in a single reckless moment — not only by the irresponsible, such as Esau, but by the sorely tried, such as Moses and Aaron."

Precept Austin provides the likely source of the phrase "a fly in the ointment" and lists biblical examples: Achan's sin (Josh. 7), Moses at Meribah (Num. 20), David with Bathsheba (2 Sam. 11), Uzziah's pride (2 Chr. 26).
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-10-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

**Tradition differences on v. 1:** The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) notes that Jerome saw in the "dead flies" wicked thoughts put into the Christian's mind by Beelzebub, "the lord of flies." This allegorical/spiritual reading is characteristic of the older church tradition. The Targum (Jewish) interprets: "evil concupiscence, which dwells at the gates of the heart, is as a fly, and is the cause of death in the world" (cited in Gill).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## v. 2 — The Heart's Inclination

**Traditional reading:** The right hand symbolizes strength, skill, and favor; the left, weakness and incompetence (the Latin *sinister* means "left"). A wise man's heart is a ready resource and guide, while a fool's heart is useless to him. Enduring Word: "Since the right hand was regarded as the side of strength, skill, and favor, the wise man's heart is known and a strength to him." Eaton (quoted ibid.): "To have one's heart at his left side is to have the 'springs of life' (Proverbs 4:23) located in the realm of practical and spiritual incompetence."

Gill: "His wisdom is ready to incline him to the right hand way for his good; but the heart of a fool to pervert him from it." The Targum applies it: "the heart of a wise man is to get the law, which was given by the right hand of the Lord; and the heart of a fool to get the goods of gold and silver."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm

---

## v. 3 — The Fool Self-Exposed

**Traditional reading:** A fool cannot hide his folly; even walking down the road, his lack of sense is evident to everyone. Gill: "his folly is manifest to all; he betrays it, by his words and actions, to every man he has to do with."

Ellicott notes an alternative reading: the Vulgate and other authorities take it as the fool, in his self-conceit, thinks everyone else is a fool. But Ellicott prefers the more obvious sense: the fool's self-betrayal (cf. Proverbs 13:16; 17:28; 18:2).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## v. 4 — Calmness Before an Angry Ruler

**Traditional reading:** If a ruler's anger flares up against you, do not abandon your position in a huff. Composure and a conciliatory spirit can pacify even great offenses. This verse echoes 8:3. Enduring Word: "Even in a difficult situation, don't leave your post. Be faithful to your position and you will find that conciliation pacifies great offenses."

Gill applies it: "leave not thy place; at court; thine office under the prince, do not throw it up in a passion, and quit his service upon it; and much less forget thy duty and allegiance to him, and go into disloyalty and rebellion." Ellicott notes that the Hebrew for "yielding" is literally "healing" (cf. Proverbs 15:4), and it "quieteth great offences" — not so much the ruler's offended feelings as the greater offences the subject might commit if he does not restrain himself.

The Targum spiritualizes: "if a spirit of evil concupiscence rules over thee; thy good place, in which thou wert used to stand, leave not" (Gill).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## vv. 5–7 — Folly Promoted, Worth Demoted

**Traditional reading:** Qoheleth observes an "evil under the sun" — an error originating from the ruler: incompetent or foolish people are promoted to high positions while the truly qualified (the "rich" in wisdom, character, or substance) are brought low. The world is often upside-down. "Servants on horseback" and "princes walking on foot" paints a vivid picture of social inversion.

Gill sees this as folly set "in great heights" — "even foolish and wicked men; men of poor extraction, of low life, and of mean abilities," while "men rich in wisdom and knowledge… rich in grace, fearing God" are neglected. Ellicott notes a historical detail: "Considering that the importation of horses was a new thing in the reign of Solomon, we look on it as a mark of later age that a noble should think himself dishonoured by having to go on foot while his inferiors rode on horseback." The Targum interprets this of Israel in exile, with Gentiles riding while Israelites walk.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/

---

## v. 8 — Digging Pits and Breaking Walls

**Traditional reading:** Those who plot against others often fall into their own traps (cf. Psalm 7:15; Proverbs 26:27). Breaking through a wall (or hedge) exposes one to hidden serpents. Gill interprets this politically: "he that breaks down the hedges and fences of kingdoms and commonwealths, and breaks through the fundamental laws of a civil constitution, and especially that transgresses the laws of God… may expect to smart for it."

Ellicott says "commentators cannot be said to have been very successful in their attempts to trace a connection between the proverbs of this chapter." He sees the common theme as "the advantage of wisdom, and here in particular of caution in great enterprises." He warns against forcing a connection to rebellion against the ruler of v. 5. The "hedge" is better understood as "a stone wall, in the crevices of which serpents often have their habitation" (cf. Amos 5:19).

Alexander Maclaren (quoted in Enduring Word) offers a spiritual application: "Whoso pulls down the wall of temperance, a serpent will bite him. Trembling hands, broken constitutions, ruined reputations, vanished ambitions, wasted lives, poverty, shame, and enfeebled will, death – these are the serpents that bite."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/

---

## v. 9 — Dangers in Honest Labor

**Traditional reading:** Even legitimate, necessary work carries risk. Quarrying stones and splitting logs are honest occupations, yet injury is always possible. Ellicott notes that "removeth" may refer to quarrying (1 Kings 5:17) rather than merely moving stones, and cleaving wood (cutting down trees) was "an operation not free from danger (Deuteronomy 19:5)." Gill extends the application: "so he that soweth discord among brethren, that makes divisions in families, neighbourhoods, kingdoms, and churches."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## v. 10 — The Dull Axe

**Traditional reading:** A practical proverb: working with a dull axe requires far more effort than sharpening it first. "Wisdom brings success" — foresight and preparation are better than brute force. Enduring Word: "The fool will continue to use a dull ax, instead of being wise and sharpening the edge. The fool doesn't wisely consider the future."

Ellicott notes the Hebrew is obscure: "The wording of this verse in the original is very obscure; and we can only say of the rendering in the text that it seems to be preferred." The Hebrew says literally "make his strength mighty." Gill: "wisdom is profitable to direct; this is the 'excellency' of wisdom, that it puts a man in the right way of doing things."

F.B. Meyer (quoted in Enduring Word) makes a devotional application to Christian workers: "There are times with all who work for God, when they are blunt, through much usage…. At all such times let us turn to God and say, 'Put in more strength. Let thy power be magnified in my weakness.'"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## v. 11 — The Serpent and the Babbler

**Traditional reading:** If a snake bites before the charmer can work his art, the charmer gains nothing. So too, the uncontrolled tongue of a babbler causes damage that cannot be undone. Ellicott provides the most detailed analysis: The Hebrew literally reads, "If the serpent bite for lack of enchantment, there is no advantage to the master of the tongue." He follows the LXX in taking "master of the tongue" to mean the snake-charmer (cf. Psalm 58:5). The phrase "master of the tongue" was deliberately chosen to lead into vv. 12–14 on speech. "Enchantment" literally means "whispering."

Gill: "a babbler is no better… a whisperer, a backbiter, a busy tattling body… such an one is like a venomous viper… there is no more guarding against him than against such a creature that bites secretly."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## vv. 12–14 — The Fool's Escalating Speech

**Traditional reading:** The wise man's words are gracious and win favor; the fool's own words destroy him. His speech starts foolish and degenerates into "evil madness" — rage, oaths, and curses. Moreover, the fool "multiplies words" — he talks endlessly, especially about the future, which no one can know.

Gill on v. 12: "The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious… He speaks well of civil magistrates… of the ministers of the word… and of all his fellow creatures." For the godly man, "his discourse will run upon the grace of God, upon the doctrines of grace, and upon the experience of the truth of grace on his heart." In contrast, "the lips of a fool swallow up himself" — his words bring ruin.

On v. 13, Gill: "as soon as ever he opens his mouth, he betrays his folly… as he goes on, he appears more and more foolish, and yet more confident of his own wisdom… if contradicted, is like a madman, scattering arrows, firebrands, and death."

On v. 14, Enduring Word: "The fool is known by his many words, and by his presumption about the future – when no man knows what is to be." The word for "fool" (*sakal*) "implies a dense, confused thinker" (Deane). Ellicott: "The fool's courageous loquacity is contrasted with the cautious silence which experience of his ignorance has taught the wise man."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/

---

## v. 15 — The Fool's Wearisome Toil

**Traditional reading:** The fool's labor exhausts him because he lacks even basic direction — "he does not know the way to the city," a proverbial saying for the most obvious, plain thing. Maclaren (in Enduring Word): "The phrase, 'how to go to the city,' seems to be a kind of proverbial comparison for anything that is very plain and conspicuous."

Kidner (ibid.): "To be ever learning, never arriving, as 2 Timothy 3:7 portrays some people, is to be a trifler who contrives to get lost on even the straightest way to the city." Gill notes that some interpret "the city" as Jerusalem where wisdom was taught; Alshech interprets it of heaven — the fool does not know the way to the heavenly city.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm

---

## v. 16 — Woe to the Land with a Childish King

**Traditional reading:** "Woe" to a land whose king is immature ("a child") and whose officials feast in the morning — starting their day with self-indulgence rather than governance. Ellicott notes the Hebrew word for "child" (*na'ar*) has a wide range: "constantly translated lad or young man," applied even to Solomon (1 Chr. 29:1) and Rehoboam (2 Chr. 13:7), and can mean "servant." Some take it as "servant" here, contrasting the nobly-born king of v. 17. But Eaton (Enduring Word) clarifies: "RSV 'is a child' refers not to age but to general maturity."

Enduring Word: "Solomon himself felt that he was but a child when he came to the throne of Israel; therefore, he wisely asked God for the wisdom to lead a great people (1 Kings 3:7-9)." Gill, whose text was partially cut off, begins: "not so much in age; though it is sometimes an unhappiness to a nation to be governed by a minor, especially if the young king has not good tutors… but, if otherwise, a nation may be very happy under a minority."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## v. 17 — Blessed is the Land with Noble Leadership

**Traditional reading:** In contrast, the land is blessed whose king is "a son of nobles" (well-born, properly trained, mature in character) and whose officials feast at the proper time — for strength to govern, not for drunkenness. The verse celebrates disciplined, purposeful leadership. Clarke (quoted in Enduring Word): "They do nothing in order; turn night into day, and day into night; sleep when they should wake, and wake when they should sleep; attending more to chamberings and banquetings, than to the concerns of the state."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/

---

## v. 18 — Laziness and Decay

**Traditional reading:** Through sloth the roof beams sag; idle hands let the house leak. This is both a literal proverb about home maintenance and a metaphor for national decline under lazy rulers. Wright (Enduring Word): "Lazy rulers bring down the great house of the nation, as a lazy householder lets the beams of his house collapse so that the roof sags and lets in the rain."

Ellicott: "droppeth — i.e., lets the rain drop through." The natural consequence of neglect in the physical realm illustrates the same principle in governance.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm

---

## v. 19 — Feasting, Wine, and Money

**Traditional reading:** This verse has provoked considerable discussion. In context, it may continue describing the foolish, self-indulgent rulers: "A feast is made for laughter, and wine makes merry; but money answers everything" — these leaders have money to fund their excesses, and they think wealth solves every problem. Ellicott takes these as "isolated proverbs" and says "the obvious meaning suggested by the English of this verse is the right one." However, he notes that "those who strive to trace a continuity of thought take Ecclesiastes 10:18 as a figurative description of the ruin of an ill-governed land; Ecclesiastes 10:19 as describing the riot of those rulers who make feasts for merriment, and have money freely at their disposal."

The statement "money answers everything" is often read as a realistic observation that in this fallen world, money is a practical tool that solves many earthly problems — not a moral endorsement of wealth. Enduring Word places it in the voice of "a wicked, unwise king" speaking.

**No prosperity gospel teaching found:** None of the accessed sources (Enduring Word, Precept Austin, Gill, Ellicott, Barnes, Pulpit Commentary) read v. 19 as a proof-text for prosperity teaching. No word-of-faith or prosperity gospel interpretation was located. The traditional readings all treat the statement either as a cynical observation from the fool's perspective or as a realistic observation about money's practical utility, not a promise of wealth.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm

---

## v. 20 — Do Not Curse the King

**Traditional reading:** Even in one's most private thoughts or bedroom, one should not curse the king or the rich, because "a bird of the air may carry your words" — secrets have a way of getting out. This is the origin of the proverb "a little bird told me." Eaton (Enduring Word): "'A little bird told me' is a proverb which appears in a variety of forms and cultures, including Aristophanes' *The Birds* and the Hittite Tale of Elkuhirsa."

Trapp (Enduring Word): "Kings have long ears, heavy hands; walls also and hedges have ears."

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word for "thought" is "a word of later Hebrew, found only in Daniel and Chronicles." He takes vv. 18–20 as part of the sequence: v. 18 describes the decay under bad rulers; v. 19 the riotous feasting of those rulers; and v. 20 warns subjects not to rebel despite the misgovernment.

The Enduring Word commentator draws a spiritual application: "A king may hear of my wrongdoing and I may suffer because of it, even though I did not know he could learn of it. The same is true of my wrongdoing before God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Readings Found

**Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes):** Gill reads the chapter primarily through a political lens — the duties of subjects toward rulers, the dangers of rebellion, and the corruption of government. His applications are practical and moral, with occasional typological connections to grace. Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary simply notes v. 1 continues 9:18 on the impact of evil.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ecclesiastes-10.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ecclesiastes-10.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Emphasizes personal application and spiritual lessons: small compromises leading to big falls, the necessity of sharpening one's spiritual "axe" through prayer, the reality that secret sins are known to God. F.B. Meyer's devotional application on the dull axe is featured. Practical, warm, application-oriented.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-10/

**Reformed/Presbyterian (JFB, Barnes):** JFB emphasizes the proportional effect of sin — "the higher a man's religious character is, the more hurt is caused by a sinful folly." Barnes treats the chapter as wisdom literature answering the question "What is good for men to do?" (2:3; 6:12), with the unifying theme of "the advantage of that wisdom which includes piety and patience."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/ecclesiastes/10.htm

**Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary):** Ellicott is cautious and scholarly, noting textual difficulties (e.g., the obscure Hebrew of v. 10, the ambiguity of v. 11), and treating many verses as isolated proverbs rather than forcing continuity. The Pulpit Commentary provides extensive philological notes and notes Jerome's allegorical reading of the "dead flies" as demonic thoughts.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/10.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-10.html

**Evangelical (Precept Austin):** Provides the most exhaustive lexical and intertextual study, with multiple Bible translations compared, Hebrew word studies, and cross-references. Emphasizes the corrupting power of "little" sins and the need for vigilance.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-10-commentary

**Lutheran (Lange's Commentary):** Views the chapter as illustrating "the superiority of wisdom over folly" in the tradition of Proverbs, with emphasis on "the insolence and haughtiness of fools, as well as their loquacity and indolent levity, in contrast to the corresponding virtues of the wise." Rejects Hengstenberg's allegorical reading of vv. 1–3 as referring to Israel groaning under Persian tyranny.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/ecclesiastes-10.html

---

## Other Views: Modern Scholarship and Catholic/Orthodox

**Catholic and Orthodox sources:** No specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentary on Ecclesiastes 10 was located in the available search results. Jerome's reading (cited in Pulpit Commentary) connecting "dead flies" to Beelzebub and wicked thoughts represents an early Church allegorical approach.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-10.html

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey):** No results were returned from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org for this chapter. However, the Precept Austin page incorporates NET Bible notes on the Hebrew text (e.g., the hendiadys in v. 1, the meaning of *yaqar* "weightier").
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-10-commentary

**Debated modern teaching (prosperity/word of faith on v. 19):** No prosperity gospel or word-of-faith interpretation of v. 19 was found in any of the accessed sources. All traditional commentators read "money answers everything" either as a cynical observation placed in the mouth of the fool or as a realistic acknowledgment of money's practical utility in a fallen world — never as a promise of wealth or a proof-text for prosperity teaching.
